anti_patterns: Direct user-to-permission grants that bypass roles (the group loophole): permissions attached to individual users cannot be reviewed as a matrix and silently survive after a job change.
One shared super-admin (a single DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE on a hot EOA): the role-admin hierarchy collapses to one key, so one compromise is a full takeover.
Role checks sprinkled through handlers with no governed grant/revoke path: membership becomes tribal knowledge and forgotten call sites stay open.
Fail-open mediation: an unknown role, a missing assignment entry, or an authorization-service error defaults to allow instead of deny.
Leaving the deployer holding DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE forever: bootstrap privilege becomes standing privilege; transfer it to a multisig/DAO and renounce the hot key.
Role explosion by cloning: MINTER_V2, MINTER_FINAL, SUPER_MINTER instead of one role plus a hierarchy or a scoped parameter - the matrix becomes unauditable.
avoid_when: A single administrator suffices: Ownable-style ownership is simpler and more honest than a one-role RBAC deployment.

Access turns on a subject-resource relationship rather than job function (attending physician of patient Y, owner of this document): use relationship- or attribute-based rules alongside or instead of roles.
No trusted identity exists yet: authenticate first, because role checks over self-asserted roles are decoration.
The check would sit in a latency-critical inner loop per element: authorize once at the boundary and carry the decision instead of re-evaluating per item.
benefits: Administration scales with jobs, not users: onboarding is a role assignment and a permission change is one grant edit, instead of hunting per-user ACLs across the system.
Reviewable access: the user-role and permission-role matrices answer 'who can do X?' and 'what can Y do?' without reading call sites, which is what audits and incident response ask for.

Separation of duties becomes structural: mutually exclusive roles (requester vs approver) are rejected at assignment time and conflicting activations at session time, instead of relying on discipline.
Least privilege by default: a subject with no role holds no permissions, and compromised keys lose power through revoke/renounce paths rather than code deploys.
Hierarchy reuse: senior roles inherit junior permissions through a partial order, so a new tier adds one inheritance edge instead of duplicated grants.
Stable vocabulary: roles track the organization's job functions, which change slowly, while users and permissions churn - so policy edits stay local to the assignment tables.
best_practices: Deny by default: no role means no permission, and unknown roles, missing entries, or decision errors all resolve to deny with an audit event.
Separate role administration from role membership: the accounts that grant roles must not be the ordinary members, and the top admin belongs to a multisig or DAO behind a timelock.
Use a two-step delayed admin transfer (propose, wait, accept, cancellable) for the root admin role so a mistyped transfer cannot brick or hand over the system.
Emit RoleGranted/RoleRevoked (or equivalent assignment-change events) and reconcile them off-chain: the event log is the audit trail and the basis for recertification.
Recertify assignments on a schedule and expire just-in-time grants: roles accumulate through history, and the effective privilege set otherwise becomes the union of every past assignment.
Encode static separation-of-duty exclusions as data (pairs of roles no subject may hold together) and check them in the grant path, not in reviewers' heads.
Keep the assignable role set small and hierarchical: prefer one role plus inheritance over cloned variants, and reach for scoped parameters or attributes before minting a new role.
Test the assignment matrix table-wise (allow and deny per role, including the empty set) plus one test proving an unassigned subject is denied on every protected operation.
context: Multi-user systems where the operations outnumber the administrators and job functions are more stable than personnel: SaaS tenants with billing/support/admin tiers, enterprise services, Kubernetes clusters, and smart contracts that split minter, pauser, upgrader, and treasury powers across admin types. Requires an authenticated subject with a verifiable identity (see authenticator) and a mediation point that every protected operation actually crosses (see authorization-enforcer): RBAC owns the assignment model - which subjects hold which roles, which permissions each role carries, who may grant roles - not the interception mechanics. When access turns on a subject-resource relationship rather than job function, roles alone are the wrong tool and need attribute or relationship rules beside them.
design_principles: All access through roles: permissions attach to roles only, never directly to subjects, so the assignment matrices stay complete and reviewable.
Complete mediation with fail-safe defaults: every protected operation checks the active-role set and denies unless a role grants it.
Least privilege: each role carries the minimum permissions its job needs, and subjects activate only the subset of roles the current session requires.
Separation of duties: conflicting powers are split across mutually exclusive roles, enforced at assignment (static) and activation (dynamic).
Least common mechanism with a small trusted admin base: role administration is itself governed by admin roles, and the root admin is the smallest, hardest-held set in the system.
intent: Mediate every permission through named roles: assign subjects to roles and permissions to roles, and authorize each operation only through the subject's active roles, so systems with multiple admin types stay least-privilege, reviewable, and cheap to administer.
name: rbac

participants.responsibility: The authenticated identity (user, service account, contract caller) that holds roles and requests operations; acquires permissions only through role membership, never directly.
A named job function (minter, pauser, admin) that groups a set of permissions; the stable vocabulary of the system, changed far less often than users or permissions.
An operation-on-object pair (mint token, pause transfers) granted to roles; the unit of authorization checked on every protected call.
The subject's activation context holding the subset of assigned roles in use right now; dynamic separation of duties constrains which roles may be active together.
The holder of a role's admin role: the only party that may grant or revoke that role. Admin roles can themselves form a hierarchy up to a root admin, so administration is governed, not ambient.

The enforcement point that resolves the subject's active roles against the permission-role map on every protected operation and denies by default; RBAC supplies the decision data, the monitor applies it.

pitfalls: Role explosion: permission combinations times environments times tenants produce hundreds of roles nobody can review; mine roles from actual job functions and use hierarchy plus scoping before minting variants.
Privilege creep: assignments are granted for incidents, migrations, and demos and never revoked, so the effective grant set becomes the union of history without recertification.
Admin-role concentration: the default admin of all roles is its own admin, so whoever holds it can grant themselves anything - it must be the hardest-held key in the system, never a hot deployer EOA.
Checking membership but not activation: a subject holds two conflicting roles and the code tests assignment instead of the session's active set, silently defeating dynamic separation of duties.
Trusting client-supplied roles: roles read from request bodies, unsigned claims, or UI state let callers widen their own permissions; resolve membership server-side from the authenticated subject.
problem: A system outgrows a single owner: minters, pausers, upgraders, moderators, and treasury operators each need different powers, and hard-coding admin checks per call site means every personnel or permission change becomes a code change, forgotten paths stay open, conflicting duties (requester vs approver) cannot be expressed, and nobody can answer 'who can do X?' without reading all the code.
quality_attributes_note: Testability 8: the assignment matrices are pure data, so allow/deny cases tabulate without I/O. Performance 8: the hot path is a set-membership test, though on-chain realizations pay per-check gas and off-chain ones pay policy-store latency. Security 8, not 10: the model enables least privilege and SoD, but a misconfigured root admin or an unwired entry point voids it. Simplicity 6 and scalability 6: role engineering, hierarchy maintenance, and recertification are the real ongoing costs.

related_patterns_notes.authentication-enforcer: Not listed as related; authenticator (below) covers the identity-proof half this pattern consumes.
related_patterns_notes.authenticator: Proves who the subject is; RBAC consumes that trusted identity and decides what it may do.
related_patterns_notes.authorization-enforcer: Owns the interception boundary (PEP/PDP wiring); RBAC supplies the assignment model - roles, grants, admin hierarchy - that the enforcer evaluates.
related_patterns_notes.complete-mediation: Requires every access to be checked; RBAC is one decision model that still needs a mediation point wired on every path to mean anything.
related_patterns_notes.least-privilege: States the minimization principle; RBAC is the mechanism that operationalizes it through roles, sessions, and revocable assignments.
related_patterns_notes.policy-guard: Wraps one operation in a focused policy predicate; RBAC centralizes reusable role assignments across all operations instead of per-call rules.
related_patterns_notes.reference-monitor: States the tamperproof, always-invoked, verifiable mediation ideal; RBAC realizations (on-chain role stores, kernel checks) are judged against it.
related_patterns_notes.security-context: Carries the authenticated subject and its attributes; RBAC resolves role membership from it but never populates it.
related_patterns_notes.subject-descriptor: Defines how a subject's roles, claims, and attributes are represented; RBAC uses that descriptor as the input to its assignment lookup.

tradeoffs: Role explosion: distinct permission combinations multiply into hundreds of roles that demand role engineering, mining, and hierarchy design to stay auditable.
Too coarse for relationship-shaped rules: 'attending physician of patient Y' needs attributes or relationships beside roles, so pure RBAC either over-grants or spawns a role per resource.

Administration is itself a target: per-role admins and a self-administering root concentrate power, and a compromised admin key re-grants anything - governance (multisig, timelock, delayed transfer) is mandatory overhead.

Assignment state has a lifecycle cost: grants must propagate, caches must invalidate on revoke, and on-chain membership either costs gas per check or surrenders on-chain enumeration to off-chain event indexing.
Static checks miss activation abuse: holding conflicting roles is only half the problem - without session/active-role tracking, dynamic separation of duties cannot be enforced.
Legibility shifts, not vanishes: handlers get cleaner, but the policy now lives in assignment tables and admin hierarchies that still need review tooling and matrix tests.
use_cases: Smart-contract systems splitting mint, burn, pause, upgrade, and treasury powers across MINTER/PAUSER/UPGRADER style roles with a governed root admin.
SaaS tenants separating billing admins, support agents, and organization owners so each tier activates only its own operations.
Kubernetes clusters binding ClusterRoles to groups via RoleBindings so platform teams audit one matrix instead of per-namespace ACLs.
DAO operations where proposer, executor, and guardian are mutually exclusive roles with timelocked administration.
Database and data-platform grants issued through role hierarchies (analyst inherits viewer) instead of per-user privilege lists.
Regulated workflows requiring requester/approver separation, where the exclusion is enforced at assignment rather than trusted to process.
